title: Lantern and Typewriter
premise: In 1917, battlefield nurse Freya Ashgrove secretly records the names of soldiers erased from official dispatches in a ledger she calls the Lantern. When a stranger named Elias Wren arrives bearing letters written in the unmistakable hand of Captain Aldous Vane — a man officially dead for a year — Freya discovers Vane is alive, hiding, and compiling evidence that senior officers falsified casualty reports to conceal a disastrous order. As the workshop where the true record is being printed comes under threat from both military police and the men it implicates, Freya must choose between loyalty to her found family of nurses and orderlies and the truth the ledger demands. The book ends with the workshop burning, the Lantern smuggled out page by page sewn into uniforms, and Freya publishing the names under a pen name years later — choosing truth at last, at the cost of everything she belonged to.
about_author: Vesper Vane is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing unsent letters from the First World War before turning to fiction. They write from a converted chapel on the coast, where they keep, they claim, one lamp lit at all times for the unnamed.

chapters.title: The Ledger of Small Lights
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. In a dressing station near Ypres, Freya records the names officers omit in her hidden ledger, the Lantern. A dying private asks her to remember him; his name never appears in dispatches. Emotional beat: quiet defiance born of grief.

chapters.title: Rules of the Ward
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Introduces the found family: Matron Cobb, orderly Tam, and fellow nurse Iris, whose loyalties to the army run deep. Freya learns to hide the ledger inside a hymnal. Beat: warmth and belonging shadowed by secrecy.

chapters.title: A Stranger at the Gate
chapters.summary: Elias Wren arrives claiming to deliver personal effects from the late Captain Aldous Vane. Freya recognizes the handwriting — identical to letters she received from a man officially dead. Beat: the first crack in her ordered world.

chapters.title: Handwriting of the Dead
chapters.summary: Freya's POV, flashback braided with present. She recalls her correspondence with Vane during her training and his reported death at Passchendaele. Elias refuses to say how he got the letters. Beat: obsession kindling.

chapters.title: What Elias Carries
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. He reveals fragments: Vane lives, wounded and hidden, gathering proof that casualty reports were falsified after a catastrophic advance order. He needs someone who can verify names. Beat: reluctant recruitment.

chapters.title: The Hymnal Question
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Iris nearly discovers the ledger while tidying Freya's kit. Freya lies for the first time to her found family. Beat: guilt — the ledger begins costing her belonging.

chapters.title: Names That Were Never There
chapters.summary: Freya cross-checks Elias's list against her own entries and finds forty-one men recorded as deserters who died in the advance. Beat: cold horror hardening into purpose.

chapters.title: The Workshop on Rue Basse
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. He brings Freya by night to a print workshop run by Belgian widow Céline Dossin, where the true account is being typeset. Beat: awe — history has an address, and it is here.

chapters.title: Céline's Types
chapters.summary: Céline's POV. Her son is among the erased names; she prints as penance and prayer. She tests Freya's commitment before letting her touch the case. Beat: another found family forming around the work.

chapters.title: Matron's Warning
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Matron Cobb, sharp-eyed, tells Freya she knows there are two kinds of nurses — those who keep rules and those who keep people — and warns her the second kind burn. Beat: love expressed as warning.

chapters.title: Letters to a Living Man
chapters.summary: Freya writes to Vane through Elias's courier chain. His reply arrives: he asks her to finish what he started if anything happens to him. Beat: intimacy across distance, dread beneath it.

chapters.title: Iris Suspects
chapters.summary: Iris's POV. Iris notices Freya's night absences and reports her suspicions not to command but to Matron, torn between duty and friendship. Beat: loyalty beginning to fracture along its seams.

chapters.title: The Inspection
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. A staff colonel inspects the station hunting a leak in casualty figures. Freya hides the ledger in plain sight inside a coffin inventory. Beat: terror sharpening her nerve.

chapters.title: Tam's Errand
chapters.summary: Tam's POV. The young orderly, eager to matter, volunteers as a courier without knowing what he carries. Beat: innocence placed unknowingly in danger — dramatic irony established.

chapters.title: Forty-One Reasons
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. She reads the forty-one families' addresses aloud to Céline as they set type. Each name becomes a face. Beat: the abstract cause made flesh.

chapters.title: The Colonel's Offer
chapters.summary: The colonel privately offers Freya a transfer home and a commendation — clearly a test or a bribe. She declines. Beat: temptation refused, stakes raised.

chapters.title: Vane, Alive and Ruined
chapters.summary: Elias smuggles Freya to meet Vane: half-blind, embittered, hiding in a flooded farmhouse. He is less a hero than a man dismantled by what he witnessed. Beat: disillusionment — the myth shrinks, the mission grows.

chapters.title: The Order That Killed Them
chapters.summary: Vane's POV. Flashback to the advance: the order sent over open ground against known machine positions, then rewritten afterward to blame the dead. Beat: righteous fury as testimony.

chapters.title: A Family Divided
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Iris confronts Freya: whatever she's doing will get people killed, including their patients. Their friendship cracks openly. Beat: loyalty vs. truth made personal.

chapters.title: The First Page Printed
chapters.summary: Céline's POV. The first finished signature of the pamphlet comes off the press. They hold it like a newborn. Beat: fragile triumph, brief joy.

chapters.title: Snow Over Passchendaele
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. A lull; Freya and Elias share a rare quiet hour and almost speak of the future neither believes in. Beat: tenderness as interlude before descent.

chapters.title: Tam Is Taken
chapters.summary: Tam is caught carrying pages and detained for questioning. He knows nothing but his fear could unravel everything. Beat: panic — the cost arrives early.

chapters.title: What Matron Knew All Along
chapters.summary: Matron Cobb reveals she has known about the ledger since chapter ten and has been covering for Freya; her own brother's name was erased in 1915. Beat: revelation re-forging the found family around shared grief.

chapters.title: Extraction of a Boy
chapters.summary: Elias and Freya engineer Tam's release by feeding the colonel a false informant. It works, but the colonel now suspects a network. Beat: victory that tightens the noose.

chapters.title: The List Grows Teeth
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Copies of the pamphlet begin circulating among leave trains; murmurs reach even the ward. Officers grow watchful. Beat: the truth gaining weight and danger together.

chapters.title: Iris Chooses
chapters.summary: Iris discovers the workshop's location and must decide: report it or warn them. She burns the note instead and says nothing — complicity as love. Beat: loyalty tipping toward truth.

chapters.title: The Colonel Closes In
chapters.summary: Colonel's POV. The colonel traces the paper stock to Rue Basse and requests authority to raid, framing it as sedition. Beat: antagonist fully armed; countdown begun.

chapters.title: Nights of Setting Type
chapters.summary: Workshop ensemble POV. Race to print the full edition before the raid everyone senses coming. Céline works until her fingers bleed. Beat: exhausted devotion.

chapters.title: Vane Comes Out of Hiding
chapters.summary: Against all advice, Vane insists on standing with the printed record and signing his testimony, knowing it signs his death warrant too. Beat: courage reclaimed from ruin.

chapters.title: The Last Signature
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Vane signs; Freya adds her ledger's final entry — her own name, as witness. Beat: identity claimed; the Lantern complete.

chapters.title: They Come at Dawn
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. The raid begins earlier than expected. Tam spots the lorries; the alarm spreads through the ward like fire. Beat: heart-pounding escalation.

chapters.title: Burning the Rue Basse
chapters.summary: Céline's POV. Rather than let the press and plates be seized, they fire the workshop. Céline watches her son's memorial go up in smoke and calls it a proper funeral. Beat: devastating sacrifice.

chapters.title: Sewn Into Uniforms
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. The surviving pages are distributed — sewn into hems, folded into bandages, carried out on leave trains by every nurse and orderly willing. Beat: the found family becoming the distribution network.

chapters.title: The Colonel's Empty Hands
chapters.summary: Colonel's POV. The raid finds ash and a hymnbook. The colonel understands he has lost but cannot say so; his report itself becomes a falsified document. Beat: ironic justice.

chapters.title: What Vane Paid
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Vane is shot attempting to draw pursuit away from the last couriers and dies in Freya's arms, asking only that the names be read aloud someday. Beat: grief transmuted into vow.

chapters.title: After the Fire
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. The station disperses: Matron reassigned, Iris posted east, Tam demobilized. The found family scatters, each carrying pages. Beat: mourning and gratitude entwined.

chapters.title: The Trial That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Freya's POV, postwar 1919. An inquiry quietly buries the pamphlet's claims, but the names have already entered private memory — families wrote back. Beat: bitter partial vindication.

chapters.title: Reading the Names Aloud
chapters.summary: Ensemble epilogue-in-motion. On the anniversary, survivors gather in a ruined chapel and read all forty-one names plus hundreds more from reconstructed copies. Beat: communal catharsis.

chapters.title: By Another Name
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Years later, Freya publishes the full record under the pen name Vesper Vane — giving Vane's witness the light of day while keeping herself hidden. Beat: truth chosen over credit.

chapters.title: One Lamp Lit
chapters.summary: Final chapter, Freya's POV, old age. In her coastal room, Freya keeps one lamp burning for the unnamed, the Lantern's last page framed above her desk. A young visitor asks why; she begins, once more, to read the names. Beat: peace — belonging found in remembrance itself.
